passage: Sit, beta, I'll tell you about your mother when she was ten. Shreya was the class monitor that year, and a thin brown dog used to sleep under the school stairs. Most children threw it a biscuit and forgot. Not Shreya. She made a chart on the back of her notebook: who brings the water bowl, who brings rotis, which day. Her friend Jaya took Tuesdays and Fridays. When the peon grumbled about the mess, Shreya and Jaya swept that corner themselves every evening before going home. By winter the dog followed the whole class to the gate. I still have that chart somewhere, folded in my cupboard.

qa.q: Where did the brown dog sleep?
qa.a: It slept under the school stairs.

qa.q: What does Shreya sweeping the corner herself suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt the dog was her class's job to look after, and she did not want the peon's complaint to end the feeding, so she fixed the mess instead of giving up.

qa.q: How could a teacher support children like Shreya who take on a job like this?
qa.a: A teacher could put the chart on the class wall and thank the helpers, so the duty is shared and does not all fall on one child.

qa.q: How might the peon have seen the dog feeding once the girls began sweeping?
qa.a: He probably found it less of a burden, since the mess was cleaned without him, and may have trusted the children more.

grounding: Illustrates a child taking steady responsibility for an animal and organising classmates into shared roles.

passage: The rain had been falling since lunch, and by four the school bus still had not come. Tanvir, eleven, had promised his teacher he would help Sarita this week, because her right arm was in a plaster and she could not carry her bag. Now the lane outside the gate was ankle-deep. He slung her bag across his chest over his own, took her umbrella in his free hand and held it over her cast instead of his head. 'Your shirt's soaked,' Sarita said. 'The plaster can't get wet. My shirt can,' he said. When the bus finally splashed up, he checked that she had a seat near the front before finding his own at the back, dripping and grinning.

qa.q: Why could Sarita not carry her own bag?
qa.a: Her right arm was in a plaster.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's reply about his shirt show about what he cared about most?
qa.a: It shows he cared more about keeping Sarita's plaster dry than about getting wet himself; he treated her comfort as his job that week. 🙂

qa.q: What small step could the school take so helpers like Tanvir are not stuck in the rain?
qa.a: The teacher could arrange a covered place to wait or a second helper, so the job stays safe and shared.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel about being helped this way?
qa.a: She might feel grateful and a little awkward, since she noticed he was getting soaked for her.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a peer-helper role he agreed to, even when heavy rain and a late bus make it harder.

passage: 'Aadhya, you and your cousin keep fighting over the one bicycle,' said Wasim Nana, 'so listen. When I was nine, my brothers and I had one cycle between three of us, and every evening ended in shouting. One night I sat with a slate and thought it through. First: who needs it most? Whoever has tuition far away. Second: the rest share by the clock, twenty minutes each, youngest first. Third: whoever breaks the rule loses the next turn. I read it out at dinner. My elder brother laughed, but my Abba said, "Try it for a week." By Thursday the shouting had stopped. I was the smallest, and I felt like a judge.'

qa.q: How long did each turn last under young Wasim's plan?
qa.a: Twenty minutes each, youngest first, after whoever had far-away tuition.

qa.q: Why did young Wasim feel like a judge?
qa.a: His rules, worked out on a slate, ended fights nobody else had solved, and even his father backed them, so the smallest brother felt important.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try with the cousin, based on this story?
qa.a: Aadhya could sit with the cousin and write a few clear, fair steps, like turns by time, and test them for a week.

qa.q: How might Wasim's elder brother have seen the plan at first?
qa.a: He laughed, so he probably thought a little boy's rules would not work, until the fights actually stopped.

grounding: Shows a child solving a daily sharing dispute with ordered, clear rules applied the same way to everyone.

passage: The lights went out at seven, just as Keerthana opened her school bag. The emergency lamp had maybe an hour of charge. Three things were due: maths sums for tomorrow, a Hindi poem to learn for Friday, and a map for next week. Her cousin Rashmi, eight, whined that they should just play in the dark. Keerthana held up three fingers. 'Rule one: tomorrow's work first. Rule two: things that need light before things that don't. Rule three: the map waits for daylight.' She finished the sums under the lamp, read the poem twice, then switched the lamp off to save charge and recited the lines in the dark while Rashmi hummed along. At eight-thirty the fan whirred back on, and she was already done.

qa.q: How many tasks were due, and which one was due tomorrow?
qa.a: Three tasks; the maths sums were due tomorrow.

qa.q: What does Keerthana holding up three fingers suggest about her mood?
qa.a: She seems calm and in charge; she wanted a plan rather than panic or play.

qa.q: Which choice worked well, and why?
qa.a: Leaving the map for daylight, because it needed light and time the lamp could not give.

qa.q: What would change if Keerthana had followed Rashmi's idea to play?
qa.a: The lamp might have run out and tomorrow's sums would still be undone.

grounding: Illustrates a child using simple ordered rules to decide what to do first during a power cut.

passage: At 7:40, in the lobby of their building in Pune, Devika held out her maths notebook. 'Just copy the last four. The bus comes in ten minutes.' Yogesh looked at the neat columns. He had left the sums for last night and then watched cartoons till dinner. His fingers actually touched the notebook. Then he pushed it back. 'Ma'am will call me to do one on the board, and I'll stand there like a statue.' He sat on the steps and did two sums fast and messily, and wrote 'will finish at lunch' beside the rest. On the bus he muttered, 'Tonight, sums before cartoons.' Devika shrugged, but she put her notebook back in her bag.

qa.q: What time was it when Devika offered her notebook?
qa.a: It was 7:40.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh push the notebook back after touching it?
qa.a: He was tempted, but he worried about being asked to solve a sum on the board, and he seemed to know copying would not fix his delay.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do so this morning rush does not happen again?
qa.a: He could stick to his own plan of sums before cartoons, doing homework soon after school.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when he refused?
qa.a: She may have felt a little brushed off, but her shrug and putting the notebook away suggest she accepted it.

grounding: Shows a child tempted to copy after putting off homework, choosing honest partial work and a new routine.

passage:
'Pooja, isn't the volcano model due Monday?'
'Papa, it's only Friday.'
'And tomorrow is Nani's birthday lunch. And Sunday you have dance.'
'...Oh.'
'So when were you planning to build it?'
'I thought Wasim was doing most of it.'
'Is that what Wasim thinks?'
Pooja picked at the sofa cushion. 'He did the drawing last week. I said I'd do the clay.'
'Then the clay is yours.'
'Can't you just make it tonight? You're good at this.'
'I'll sit with you. Your hands, though, not mine.'
She groaned, then went to find the clay. 'Fine. But you hold the bottle when we test it.'
'Deal. Call Wasim first and tell him honestly where it stands.'

qa.q: When is the volcano model due?
qa.a: It is due on Monday.

qa.q: What does Pooja picking at the cushion suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She likely felt a bit guilty as she realised she had not done her share of the project.

qa.q: How did Papa support her without doing the work for her?
qa.a: He helped her see how little time was left and offered to sit with her, but insisted on her own hands and on being honest with Wasim.

qa.q: If you were Wasim, what would you want from Pooja?
qa.a: I would want her to do the clay she promised and tell me honestly if she was behind, so Monday is not a surprise.

grounding: Shows a child's procrastination on a shared project and a parent steering her toward doing her own part honestly.

passage: Class 4B shop day, teacher's note. Each child had twenty paper tokens to spend at the classroom stalls. Thomas walked the whole room before buying anything. He asked Rafiq, who ran the pencil stall, why an eraser cost three tokens and a sharpener five. Rafiq explained that the sharpener 'has a blade, so it's more work to make.' Thomas nodded slowly. He bought one sharpener, skipped the paper sweets, and kept twelve tokens 'for next month's shop day.' Later I heard him tell Rafiq, 'You're good at prices.' Next step: I will let Thomas and Rafiq plan the prices together for the next shop day, and ask the whole class to find out what a few things cost at home.

qa.q: How many tokens did each child have?
qa.a: Each child had twenty tokens.

qa.q: What does Thomas's comment to Rafiq suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed to admire how Rafiq understood why things cost what they did.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's next step a good way to support this?
qa.a: Planning prices lets the boys practise judging what things are worth, and asking about home links tokens to real money.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt when Thomas praised his prices?
qa.a: He likely felt proud and noticed, since his explanation had been taken seriously. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child treating tokens as value to compare and save rather than spend on everything at once.

passage: Dear diary, today Jasleen got a new sparkly pencil box AGAIN. Her old one is fine, only the zip is stuck. I wanted to cry a bit because mine is the one Didi used. At home I counted my tin. Ninety-two rupees. The box costs one hundred and fifty. Mummy said if I want, I can put in ten rupees every Sunday and it will take six Sundays. Six!! Then I tried the candle trick on my old zip, like Nanaji showed me, and it slides now. So maybe I will save for the storybook instead. Don't know yet. Also Jasleen threw away a notebook with half the pages empty. I took it. Rough work for a month, free. – Indu

qa.q: How much money was in Indu's tin?
qa.a: Ninety-two rupees.

qa.q: Why did Indu feel like crying at first?
qa.a: Indu wanted a shiny new box like Jasleen's, but Indu's own box was a hand-me-down from Didi.

qa.q: What could Mummy do to keep supporting Indu's saving?
qa.a: Mummy could help Indu keep track of the Sunday savings so Indu sees the goal get closer, and let Indu choose between the box and the book.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see the notebook Indu took?
qa.a: Jasleen probably saw it as used and not worth keeping, while Indu saw a month of free rough paper.

grounding: Shows a child counting savings toward a goal, repairing instead of replacing, and reusing what others waste.

passage: On Monday mornings at their school in Cape Town, the flag went up while the anthem played through a crackly speaker. Thabo, ten, took off his cap and stood still, even though his shoelace was undone. Yara, who had arrived from Jordan in March, whispered, 'Why does everyone go so quiet?' Thabo waited for the last note. 'My gogo says it's for everyone who worked to make this country fair,' he whispered back. 'She was there when it changed.' Yara thought about it. At lunch she drew her own country's flag in her notebook and showed him. Thabo studied it carefully. 'Teach me what the colours mean,' he said, 'and I'll teach you the words of ours.'

qa.q: Where was Thabo's school?
qa.a: It was in Cape Town.

qa.q: Why did Thabo stand still even with his shoelace undone?
qa.a: He felt the anthem deserved his respect, partly because his gogo connected it with people who worked to make the country fair.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on the swap Thabo suggested?
qa.a: A teacher could invite children to share the flags and songs of their families' countries, so respect for symbols includes everyone's.

qa.q: What might the flag moment feel like for Yara as a newcomer?
qa.a: It may have felt confusing at first, then more welcoming once Thabo explained and asked about her own flag. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child honouring the national flag and anthem, linked to a grandparent's story, and respecting a classmate's flag too.

passage: The day before Republic Day, the scouts' room smelled of starch and marigolds. Arohi, twelve, and Gurpreet had been chosen to fold the flag so it would open cleanly at the ceremony. Gurpreet swung one corner round his shoulders like a cape. 'Superhero!' Arohi caught the cloth before it brushed the floor. 'Not on the ground. Sir said.' 'It's just practice.' 'Still.' She showed him how the petals go inside the last fold, the way the scout teacher had shown them, slowly, twice. Gurpreet stopped fooling and copied her. When the teacher checked, the bundle held. 'Good,' he said. 'Who noticed it nearly touched the floor?' Gurpreet, a little red, pointed at Arohi. 'She did.'

qa.q: What was placed inside the last fold?
qa.a: Petals were placed inside the last fold.

qa.q: Why did Arohi catch the cloth so quickly?
qa.a: She seems to feel the flag deserves care and wanted to keep the rule the teacher gave, even during practice.

qa.q: What made Arohi's correction work?
qa.a: She did not scold; she showed him the proper fold slowly, which gave him a way to join in.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt when he pointed at Arohi?
qa.a: Probably a bit embarrassed about his joke, but honest enough to give her the credit.

grounding: Illustrates a child treating the national flag with respect during a school ceremony rehearsal and following the school's rule.

passage: Every Saturday in their block in Kraków, the courtyard bins overflowed, and the neighbours blamed each other. Jana, nine, noticed pizza boxes stuffed whole into the paper bin, blocking it. Some were her family's. She fetched scissors, flattened them, and showed her little sister Dalia how the pieces slid in easily. 'That's not our job,' Dalia said. 'Half of it is,' said Jana. Then she wrote a sign in careful letters, PLEASE FLATTEN BOXES. THANK YOU!, and taped it to the lid with a small drawing of a smiling box. By the next Saturday, Mr. Nowak from the ground floor was flattening his too, and he waved at Jana from his window.

qa.q: What did Jana write on the sign?
qa.a: PLEASE FLATTEN BOXES. THANK YOU!

qa.q: What did Jana mean by 'Half of it is', and what does it show about her?
qa.a: She was admitting some of the mess was her own family's, so she felt it was fair to fix it rather than blame the neighbours.

qa.q: Why did the sign work better than complaining would have?
qa.a: It was friendly, clear and showed an easy fix, so neighbours could copy her without feeling accused.

qa.q: How might Mr. Nowak have seen Jana after the sign went up?
qa.a: His wave suggests he appreciated her effort and felt friendlier towards her.

grounding: Shows a child owning her share of a shared courtyard problem and caring for a community space.

passage: In the computer lab, while the teacher helped someone at the back, Ojas nudged Sahil. On his screen was a photo he had taken at lunch: a classmate asleep on his desk, mouth open. 'Class group, yes? Everyone will laugh so hard.' Sahil, eleven, did laugh for a second. Then he pictured his own face up there. 'Delete it, yaar.' 'It's a joke.' 'He didn't say yes to the joke.' Ojas rolled his eyes, then sighed and dragged the photo to the bin. 'Empty the bin too,' Sahil said. Ojas did. 'Now let's finish the chart before Sir checks,' Sahil said, pulling the keyboard closer, his hands still a little shaky.

qa.q: What was in the photo Ojas wanted to share?
qa.a: A classmate asleep on his desk with his mouth open.

qa.q: What does Sahil picturing his own face suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: He imagined how it would feel to be the one laughed at, which turned his laugh into concern.

qa.q: How could a teacher support what Sahil did?
qa.a: A teacher could talk with the class about asking before sharing anyone's photo, and quietly thank students who stop a post like this.

qa.q: What would change for the sleeping classmate if the photo had been posted?
qa.a: He might have been teased in front of the whole class without ever agreeing to it.

grounding: Illustrates respectful digital behaviour, a child stopping a friend from sharing a classmate's photo without consent.

passage:
Dear Baljeet Bhaiya,
You asked how the physics prelims went. Badly, but here's the strange part. When I got the paper back, I didn't just stare at the marks. I sat on the terrace and went through each wrong answer and asked, 'What was I thinking here?' Three mistakes were the same. I read half the question, felt sure I knew it, and started writing. So it isn't that I don't know physics. It's that I trust my first guess too fast. That was annoying to see. Now I'm trying something: I underline what the question actually asks before I pick up the pen. It took longer in yesterday's test, but I only lost two marks. Did you do anything like this in college?
Ojas

qa.q: How many of Ojas's mistakes were the same kind?
qa.a: Three of the mistakes were the same kind.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when he spotted the pattern in his mistakes?
qa.a: Ojas found it annoying to see, but it also changed how Ojas saw the problem: rushing, not not knowing physics.

qa.q: What would you advise Ojas to add to his new habit?
qa.a: Ojas could jot down mistake types after each test and check whether underlining keeps working.

qa.q: How might Baljeet Bhaiya see this letter?
qa.a: He might feel trusted that Ojas is asking him, and could share his own study habits from college.

grounding: Shows a teenager examining the pattern behind their own errors and adjusting the approach.

passage: 'Okay, Jyoti, don't laugh. You know the debate last week? I lost, and I was so angry I replayed it in bed. Somewhere around midnight I noticed something weird. Every time the other side made a good point, my brain didn't even consider it. It just jumped to, how do I knock this down? Like, I wasn't listening, I was loading. I do that with my dad too, now that I think about it. So yesterday I tried to catch it. When Sir said "I disagree, Naveen" in class, I made myself count to three and repeat his point in my head first. It felt slow and kind of silly. But I actually changed my answer halfway. That has never happened before.'

qa.q: When did Naveen notice his habit?
qa.a: Around midnight, while replaying the lost debate in bed.

qa.q: What does 'I wasn't listening, I was loading' show about how Naveen now sees his own mind?
qa.a: Naveen realises the thinking was set on winning rather than understanding, and seems a little uneasy admitting it.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen, and how could he build on it?
qa.a: Counting to three and restating the other person's point helped; Naveen could try the same thing in arguments with Dad.

qa.q: How might Jyoti react to hearing this?
qa.a: Jyoti might be surprised and respect Naveen more, since Naveen is owning a flaw instead of blaming the judges. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teenager noticing how his own mind reacts in arguments and trying a new way to think.

passage: I'm Manjula, and my sister Uma is fifteen. She can't just sit through a power cut. Last Sunday, when the lights went, she lay on the floor and started: 'What if the power never came back? The whole city, for a year?' I said we'd buy candles. She said candles run out, and then what about the water pumps, and the fridges at the vegetable market, and hospitals. She got a notebook and made columns: first week, first month, first year. Her face was serious, but I'm not sure if she was scared or just enjoying it. When the fan came back on, she kept writing for another hour. At dinner she asked Papa if our building has a generator. He said yes, and she looked almost disappointed.

qa.q: What columns did Uma make in her notebook?
qa.a: First week, first month and first year.

qa.q: What might Uma's almost disappointed look at dinner suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was enjoying working through the imagined scenario, and the generator closed one branch of it, though Manjula can't be sure.

qa.q: How could a parent support Uma's what-if thinking?
qa.a: Papa could ask follow-up questions about her columns or suggest she turn them into a story or project, instead of just closing the question.

qa.q: How does Manjula see Uma's habit?
qa.a: She seems amused and a little puzzled, unsure whether Uma is scared or having fun.

grounding: Shows a teenager building a detailed imagined scenario from a what-if question, seen by her sister.

passage:
Monday: Anand sat in the canteen listing questions for Saturday's school trek. What if it rains on the ridge? What if the bus is late and we lose light? What if someone's shoe sole comes off? Jaya laughed. 'You're planning a disaster movie.' He shrugged and packed spare plastic bags and a roll of tape anyway.
Saturday: Clouds rolled in by eleven. Everyone's phones went into Anand's bags, and when a classmate's sole flapped loose, he taped it. Seeing the dark sky, the teacher took the shorter path Anand had asked her about earlier in the week.
Sunday: Jaya texted: 'Okay, disaster-movie boy. Help me plan the science fair. What could go wrong?' 😅

qa.q: What did Anand pack after Jaya teased him?
qa.a: Spare plastic bags and a roll of tape.

qa.q: What does Jaya's Sunday message suggest about how her view changed?
qa.a: She still teases him, but she now trusts his what-if thinking enough to ask for his help.

qa.q: What made Anand's imagining useful rather than just worrying?
qa.a: He turned each what-if into a small practical preparation and a question for the teacher.

qa.q: How might the classmate with the loose sole have felt on Saturday?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful, since the tape let them keep walking.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager imagining scenarios that have not happened yet and preparing for them.

passage: 12 Aug. Park flooded again. Yusuf says it's just too much rain. But it rained this much last year and the swings were fine. So after school we walked around it like detectives. 1) The new building next door has covered its whole plot in cement, so water can't soak in. 2) The drain near the gate is full of chip packets. 3) The gardener cut back the hedge, and now soil slides onto the path and into the drain. Any one of these alone maybe wouldn't matter. Together the water has nowhere to go, and now there are mosquitoes, so Ammi won't let my little brother out. Yusuf said I'm overthinking. Maybe. I'm going to draw arrows between all of these tonight. – Kashish

qa.q: What was blocking the drain near the gate?
qa.a: Chip packets were blocking it.

qa.q: Why does Kashish want to draw arrows tonight?
qa.a: Kashish believes the flooding comes from the causes working together, and wants to see how they connect.

qa.q: What could Kashish do next with these findings?
qa.a: Kashish could show the drawing to the colony committee or a teacher, so the adults who manage the drain and park can act.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see the problem differently?
qa.a: Yusuf sees one simple cause, heavy rain, and thinks Kashish is making it complicated.

grounding: Shows a teenager tracing how several separate causes combine to flood a park and affect the family.

passage:
Kishore: canteen line was 20 min again 😠
Devika: ya bcoz one counter

qa.q: Why is Kishore's plan stronger than just adding a counter?

passage: Varun had been sure since Monday: the new chemistry teacher disliked him. She had cut four marks on his practical file, and he told everyone at the Salt Lake bus stop. On Thursday, Deepika showed him her file. Four marks cut too, for the same missing diagrams. 'She wrote the same comment on mine,' Deepika said. Varun felt his face heat up. He opened his file again and actually read the red ink. It was specific, even polite. 'I think I decided she hated me because I felt bad,' he said slowly, 'and then I only noticed things that fit.' Deepika grinned. 'So, apologise to the bus stop?' 'Maybe just redraw the diagrams first.'

qa.q: How many marks were cut from Varun's file?
qa.a: Four marks were cut.

qa.q: What made Varun's face heat up?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed once Deepika's file showed the same cut and comment, proving his story about the teacher was wrong.

qa.q: What habit could help Varun next time he feels treated unfairly?
qa.a: He could read the actual feedback and compare with others before deciding someone is against him.

qa.q: What would change if Varun had kept telling his story at the bus stop?
qa.a: Other students might have started seeing the teacher as unfair without reason, hurting her start at the school.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising that his hurt feelings shaped his belief and that he only noticed evidence that fit it.

passage:
'Auto is always faster than the bus to Nani's. Always.'
'Payal, last week the auto took forty minutes,' said her brother Amandeep, not looking up from his laptop.
'That was one time. Traffic.'
'And the one time you took the bus?'
'...It came quickly. But that was luck.'
'So when the auto is slow, it's traffic, and when the bus is fast, it's luck?'
Payal opened her mouth, then closed it. 'Okay, that sounds bad when you say it.'
'I'm not saying the bus is faster. I don't know either.'
'Then why are you arguing?'
'I'm not. I'm asking how you know.'
She thought. 'I don't, really. I just hate the bus because it's crowded.'
'That's a real reason. Just not a speed reason.'
'Fine. Let's time both next month.'

qa.q: How long did the auto take last week?
qa.a: It took forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Payal realise when she said 'that sounds bad when you say it'?
qa.a: She realised she had been explaining away evidence that did not fit her belief, and felt a bit caught out.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's approach get right?
qa.a: He asked how she knew instead of claiming the opposite, which let her find the flaw herself.

qa.q: What would change if Amandeep had just said 'you're wrong'?
qa.a: Payal would likely have dug in and defended the auto instead of admitting she didn't really know.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager noticing that dislike of the bus, not evidence, was driving her certainty, and admitting what she does not know.
